Sh V.P.S Chaudhary, Food Inspector was examined as PW-1.
PW-1 in his examination-in-chief stated that on 05.11.2010 he had visited the shop of the accused where accused Jagjit Singh was found conducting the business of sale of 'Coconut Laddoo'.

As per PW-1 after disclosing his identity, he purchased 1500 grams of coconut Laddoo from an open aluminum tub having no label declaration, after properly mixing with the help of clean and dry spoon in a clean and dry tray.
As per PW-1 he paid Rs.150/- vide vendors receipt Ex.PW1/A as sample price.
As per PW-1 after lifting of sample, it was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed in clean and dry glass bottles.
As deposed by PW-1, vendor signatures were obtained on the LHA slip.
Thereafter, one counter part of the sample was deposited with the public analyst (PA) on 06.11.2010 and remaining two counterparts were deposited with the LHA.

PW-1 further deposed that on receipt of the PA report Ex PW1/H the sample was found to be adulterarted, thereafter he sent a letter ExPW1/H to STO Ward No. 99 to disclose the constitution of M/s Jagjit Halwai shop.
As per reply received, no such firm of the accused was found registered with the Sales Tax.
PW-1 further deposed that after obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA the present complaint was filed against the accused person.

ARGUMENTS 11.

Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, as all the witnesses have supported the case and there is no contradiction in their testimony.

It is further submitted that the accused has failed to rebut the findings as given by the PA in his report Ex.PW1/G and neither the said NABEELA WALI WALI CC Complainant vs Sh. Jagjit Singh on 17 December, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105437903/

12. On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. Counsel for the accused that the food article i.e. Coconut Laddu would fall under the category of sweet as mentioned under Appendix B of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rule 1995 under the heading of "A.25 SWEETS AND CONFECTIONERY".
It is further argued that since the said category of food permits the usage of edible oils and fats hence there was no occasion for the Public Analyst to test the product for vegetable oil.
Also it is argued that it was wrongly concluded that the food product in question was adulterated because of the presence of the vegetable oil, as vegetable oil is not injurious to health.
It is also argued by Ld. Counsel for the accused the the BR test conducted by the Food Analyst is prescribed only to find out the adulteration in vegetable oils.

It is argued that since edible oils including vegetable oil is permitted in sweets,
hence the test was wrongly applied by the Food Analyst.
13.

It is also argued by Ld. Counsel for the accused person that it is not clear as to how the Food Analyst came to know about the ingredients of the food article, as copy of Form VI which mentions the constituents of the food article as declared by the accused was not provided to the Food Analyst and only Form VII as per rules was sent to the Food Analyst.

It is also argued NABEELA Digitally signed by NABEELA WALI WALI Date: 2022.12.17 17:22:17 +0530 CC No:- 44283/2016 DA (FSO)
v. Jagjit Singh. Page No. 7 of 14 that the adulteration as stated in the PA report does not fall under Section 2(1a)(a)(b) &(m) for which the complaint has been filed against the accused.
It is further argued that as per circular dated 19.07.2021 FSSAI coconut ladoo can only be tested for contaminants, microbiological requirements and additives allowed to be used.

14. To begin with it is an admitted fact that a sample of Coconut ladoo was lifted by the food officials on 05.11.2010 from the said premises and the accused was the vendor who had sold the said article.
It is not his stand that the food article was not for sale or that it was for any purpose other than sale for human consumption.
No defect or irregularity in the sample proceedings has been raised by the defence.
There is no dispute about the sample having been sent to the PA on the specified date in question.

There is also no dispute that the complaint was filed as per the procedure after obtaining sanction / consent of the Director, PFA.
15.
It is then seen that the accused has not questioned the fact that the business concern M/s. Jagjit Halwai was a proprietorship concern, of which he was the proprietor.

It is not his case that he was not the proprietor of the said premises or that some NABEELA by NABEELA WALI WALI Date:

He rather admitted this fact in his statement under section 313 CrPC.

It is then seen that the accused has not exercised his right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting that sample analysed through CFL.
16.

It is also pertinent to note that the accused has not questioned the correctness of the PA report (though has disputed his opinion that the food article was adulterated due to presence of vegetable oil) in the sample.

Although during cross- examination of PW-1, Ld. Counsel for accused had given suggestion regarding presence of ghee in the tray in which the coconut ladoo was kept but during final arguments the Ld. Counsel for accused took a different stand and admitted presence of Complainant vs Sh. Jagjit Singh on 17 December, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105437903/

17. It is to be understood that the notice framed upon the accused is for violation of Section 2(ia)(a),(b) and (m) of the PFA Act.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.

Under section 2(ia)(b) of PFA NABEELA WALI WALI Date:
2022.12.17 17:22:30 +0530 CC No:- 44283/2016 DA (FSO) v. Jagjit Singh. Page No.
9 of 14 Act, it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof.

On the other hand,
section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.

18. Considering the first argument, a careful perusal of the entry A.25 Sweets & Confectionery under Appendix B shows that although the entry is titled as 'Sweets & Confectionery' the relevant entry deals with sugar boiled confectionery or pan goods confectionery like toffee etc.
No other entry under Appendix B talks of Coconut Ladoo or sweets as such.
Thus 'coconut laddu' does not fall under any item of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules.

The PA report also does not mention any item no.
under Appendix B under which the said item falls.
Thus 'coconut laddo' is not a standdised food article and thus, no standards have been prescribed under the Rules with respect to 'coconut laddu'.
19. On the other hand, proprietary Food, as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules means a food which has not been standardised under the said Rules.

Under Rule 37-A, proprietary food products shall NABEELA WALI WALI Date:
2022.12.17 17:22:36 +0530 CC No:- 44283/2016 DA (FSO) v. Jagjit Singh.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

Page No.
10 of 14 not contain food additives except as provided under the rules for that food or category of food.
20. In the present case as is described, the food article would fall under the category of proprietary food under Rule 37-A of the Prevention of Adulteration Rules.
Thus, it is clear that the food article "coconut laddu" is not a standardised food article and thus, no standards have been prescribed under the PFA Rules which can be said to have been violated.
Since no standards have been prescribed for this commodity, it would be clear that section 2(ia)(m) of the PFA Act would not apply.
Such provision would be applicable only where the quality or purity of a food article falls below the prescribed standards.
But when there are no standards prescribed, there can be no violation under section 2(ia)(m).
But to say, that since there are no standards for this food article and thus there can be no adulteration, would certainly be not correct.
Even if a food article is not a standardised food article, it has to be free from adulteration and has to pass the other tests upon being considered as a proprietary food.

It cannot be said that since there are no standards prescribed for a particular food article, a seller is free to add poison/insects/putrid substance to it or Complainant vs Sh. Jagjit Singh on 17 December, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105437903/
6 sell it by injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.

The only benefit which the accused can Digitally get signed in case of such by NABEELA NABEELA WALI WALI Date:
2022.12.17 17:22:43 +0530 CC No:- 44283/2016 DA (FSO) v. Jagjit Singh.

Page No.
11 of 14 proprietary food is that there cannot ordinarily be a violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act which pertains to violation of prescribed standards.
Also it is not the case of the prosecution that the purchaser/FSO had demanded a food article of special nature, substance and quality and the article sold was not such.

Hence,
concurring with the submission of Ld. Defence Counsel there is also no violation under Section 2(ia)(a) of the Act.
21.
As per the PA report Ex.PW1/H, the sample is adulterated due to presence of vegetable oil.
The presence of vegetable oil is also not disputed by the accused.

Thus, if the arguments of the Ld.
Counsel for the accused is considered and the food article is presumed to fall under the category of sweets and confectionery even then as per the report of the Public Analyst which is Ex.PW1/H, the BR test reading for the edible oil used in the food article is mentioned as 39.5 which is above the prescribed standards of 34 to 35.5.

Thus even if, it is assumed that the edible oil used in the food article was permitted, the quality of the edible oil as per the PA report is not up to the mark and hence resultantly makes the food article unsafe.

Also in view of the above discussion the argument of the Ld. Counsel for the accused that the copy of Form VI was not provided to the Food Analyst and only Form VII was sent does not require discussion on merit.

NABEELA  WALI
WALI Date: 2022.12.17  17:22:48 +0530 CC No:- 44283/2016 DA (FSO) v. Jagjit Singh.
Page N 22.

As far as the last argument of the Ld. Counsel with respect to order dated 19.07.2021 of FSSAI is concerned, it is pertinent to mention that the present complaint has been filed under the PFA Act and Section 97 of the FSSA clearly protects the operation of relevant Section under PFA.

Moreover,
as is well established the provision of law would have a riding effect over any administrative office order.
23. The prosecution is required to prove its case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt and not to prove the case beyond all remotest probabilities and possibilities.

Of course there are several defences available to the accused, but the prosecution is not required to rule out all the said remote possibilities and defences under the sun which the accused might claim at the trial.

If any specific defence has been taken by the accused, it would be for the accused to establish the same by either pointing out the defects / infirmities in the prosecution case and / or by leading defence evidence.
But the accused cannot claim that all the remote possibilities have to be ruled out by the prosecution.

7 24.
In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

Thus accused namely Jagjit Singh S/o Sh. Kaleecharan is convicted for the violation of abovestated provisions.
